title: May's Moonless Nights Are Your Best Chance to See the Milky Way's Glowing Heart
summary: Imagine looking up and seeing a shimmering river of stars stretching across the sky. That's the Milky Way, our home galaxy, and mid-May is one of the best times to spot its bright, busy center. Why? Because the moon takes a little break. During the new moon in May, the sky is at its darkest, and the Milky Way's core shines like a glowing arch. You'll need to stay up late—or wake up super early. The best viewing is between midnight and dawn, when the galaxy's heart is highest in the sky. Head to a place far from city lights, like a dark sky park. Then face south. You'll see the dense core passing through constellations like Sagittarius and Scorpius. It looks like a fuzzy band of light, but it's actually made of billions of stars, gas, and dust. If you want to take pictures, a good camera with a wide lens can capture colors your eyes can't see. Apps like Stellarium can help you plan exactly when and where to look. Remember, the June new moon comes too close to summer, when twilight lingers and steals the darkness. So May is your golden ticket. Grab a blanket, find a dark spot, and let your eyes adjust. You might even spot a shooting star while you're at it. The universe is putting on a show—don't miss it!
why_it_matters: May's dark night skies offer a perfect chance for kids to see the Milky Way and feel a sense of wonder about the vast galaxy we live in, right from their own backyard.

background_read: The Milky Way is our home galaxy—a huge spiral collection of stars, gas, and dust that we see as a bright band across the night sky.
The constellations Sagittarius (which looks like a teapot) and Scorpius (a scorpion shape) mark the area where the galaxy's bright center shines.
Dark sky parks are special areas where artificial lights are limited so people can see the stars clearly, and they are great places to view the Milky Way.
Article_Structure: WHO: Stargazers and anyone who wants to see the Milky Way
WHAT: The best chance to see the glowing center of the Milky Way is during the new moon in May, between midnight and dawn
WHERE: In dark places away from city lights, facing south toward the constellations Sagittarius and Scorpius
WHY: Because the May new moon provides the darkest skies and the core is high in the sky at the right time, while in June twilight interferes

perspectives.description: Amateur astronomers love May because it gives them the darkest skies to capture stunning photos of the Milky Way.
Light pollution from cities is making it harder for many people to experience truly dark skies, which highlights the need to protect dark spaces.
The timing of moon phases and seasons determines when certain stars and constellations are visible, and May's alignment is just right this year.
